content: The relationship between immune markers and protection is complex. A 0 log antibody titre is associated with 100% protection, but variations in antibody distributions and why a specific titre might only provide 70% protection are discussed in detail. Nauta et al. demonstrated, using influenza vaccination as an example, that the relationship between antibody titres and clinical protection in a population depends not only on the mean titre but also on the standard deviation of the log-transformed antibody titres. This highlights the need to consider both parameters when generalizing findings from one population to another. Threshold methods assume a step-function relationship, where individuals with immune marker levels above a certain threshold are fully protected, while those below remain fully susceptible. These methods align with the Prentice criteria, assuming the threshold is consistent across vaccinated and unvaccinated individuals. For example, Chen et al. identified a PRN titre >120 mIU/mL as a surrogate for protection against measles, as no individuals with titres above this threshold developed clinical measles during an outbreak. Similar thresholds have been identified for diseases like diphtheria and rubella. Another approach involves estimating vaccine efficacy (VE) by comparing the proportions of vaccinated and unvaccinated individuals below specific immune marker thresholds. This method uses the traditional equation for clinical VE and assumes a step-function relationship between immune markers and susceptibility. For instance, Siber et al. described deriving VE from immune marker titres graphically, using reverse cumulative distributions of log-transformed titres in vaccinated and unvaccinated groups. Continuous methods, on the other hand, relate immune marker titres to disease risk without assuming a specific protective threshold. For example, regression models have been used to describe the association between pre-exposure antibody titres and disease incidence, allowing for VE estimation. Chan et al. used such models to infer clinical protection after varicella vaccination, while Storsaeter et al. developed a logistic regression model to quantify the relationship between pertussis antibodies and vaccine-derived protection. Host factors, such as age, also influence immune responsiveness and protection. For example, immune system changes over the lifespan, including the acquisition and loss of maternal antibodies, immune maturation in early childhood, and immunosenescence in old age, can affect the components of the immune response predictive of VE. Studies have shown that while serum HI antibody titres predict influenza vaccine efficacy in younger individuals, cell-mediated immunity (CMI) may be a better predictor in older adults. Socioeconomic status and environmental factors also play a role in the relationship between immune markers and protection. Variations in exposure intensity, such as those seen in crowded or deprived settings, can influence the level of protection provided by a specific antibody titre. For example, higher antibody titres may be required in populations with greater exposure to infectious agents. In summary, the relationship between immune markers and vaccine efficacy is influenced by multiple factors, including population heterogeneity, exposure intensity, host factors, and the specific clinical endpoint being evaluated. These complexities must be considered when predicting vaccine performance or using immune markers as surrogates for clinical protection.
